# Related Works 

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in sports, specifically, has led to a larger area of research. This chapter reviews articles to show how CaddySense stands with the ideas of AI coaching technologies, performance modeling, and human with AI interaction. Instead of simply listing findings, this review will highlight how these words are related to one another, and where they are similar and different. This project will also show where the gaps are that they explain in the works. Throughout the chapter, it will demonstrate and show how these scholarly sources are playing into ideas about the conceptual, technical, and ethical foundations of CaddySense, but also show opportunities for a system that is designed for all kinds of golfers. 

## Overview of AI in Sports

Earlier work in AI-based sports coaching is mainly focused on structured rule-based systems that were designed to help with narrowing training tasks. In their work, Novatchkov and Baca (2013) describe this foundation through a weight training system that relied on an approach called explicit-encoded logic, limited sensor integration, and predefined feedback rules [@Novatchkov2013_AIinWeightTraining]. These systems were innovative for their time, however relatively static. This means that they were not able to generalize, adapt, or even personalize feedback beyond what their programmer originally designed. Many current systems work more as as expert simulators rather than adaptive coaches. Zhou (2025) highlights in their review that they are mirror logic, but lack the ability to learn directly from athlete performance and behavior [@Zhou2025_AIinSportNarrativeReview]. Table 1 below summarizes the progression of how AI has shifted from rough systems to a more adaptive, data-driven model, which supports the claim that modern tools like Caddysense must focus on these evolutions. Huang et al. (2024) also explains that AI integration in sports coaching can lead to training improvement and also prevent injuries, while also focusing on challenges that are directly tied to system accessibility [Huang2024_IntegrationAIinSportsCoaching]. Li et al. (2025) wrote a reveiw of AI in apps in sports, which looking into how more modern systems are able to combine data , machine learning, and other user-ceneted design to deal with athletic performance and training [Li2025_AIinSportsTechnologiesReview].

Table: Evolution of AI in Sports Technology

| Year      | Description                                                                           |
|:----------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2010-2014 | Rule-based systems Models often use handwritten logic and limited sensors             |
| 2015-2018 | First look at machine learning, data-driven feedback, smaller scope                   |
| 2019-2022 | Deep learning grows into player tracking, prediction, and injury modeling             |
| 2023-2025 | Modern AI uses data,decision support, and complex reasoning                           |

Other reviews show that the field overall has evolved significantly. In their narrative analysis, Zhou (2025) emphasizes that multimodal data streams, deep learning architectures, and applications that go beyond performance measurement in order to include automated strategy analysis, things like fatigue monitoring, and predictive injury models. In their narrative review, for example, they talk and emphasize a shift from symbolic to data-driven AI have allowed systems to perform with more efficiency and contextual awareness [@Zhou2025_AIinSportNarrativeReview]. Similarly, Pietraszewski et al. (2025) explain something that they call trace performance analytics, which trends across many athlete populations and their competitive contexts. Their analysis shows that AI is more efficient when it's integrated across many dimensions of performance, rather than targeting isolated metrics [@Pietraszewski2025_RoleAIinSportsAnalytics]. Table 2 showcases the differences with the earlier set systems with more modern deep-learning models. This can help in the understanding of why current tools need to be adaptable, which is crucial for CaddySense.

Table: Key differences between rule-based systems and more modern deep learning AI in sports.

| Feature                | Rule-Based AI                        | Deep Learning AI                                |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| Data Requirement       | Low - predefined logic               | High - needs large amounts of labeled data      |
| Adaptability           | Low - can not adjust without updates | High - models self adjust and learn patterns    |
| Real Time Feedback     | Limited, static                      | Strong - context aware output                   |
| Personalization        | Manual, runs off rules               | Automatic - learns from user data/behavior      |
| Performance Prediction | Weak, too linear                     | Strong - predictive model capability            | 

These more modern reviews can also be seen as similar to the work of Raturi (2024), who argues that the future look of AI in coaching really depends on the ability to be able to support real-time choice making, rather than only providing summaries afterward. On the other hand, after reviewing all of these studies, researchers note that more complicated systems are still unevenly targeted at high-performance athletes. Raturi (2024) further points out that more recreational athletes usually lack the level of treatment that the higher-level athletes are receiving [@Raturi2024_AIinSportsTrainingOverview]. Out of all of these studies, these researchers note that sophisticated systems still favor elite athletes. Recreational users are still at a disadvantage. This further shows the research gap CaddySense will attempt to address. This particular gap is more clearly seen in golf, as most of the data-driven tools focus on professional swing metrics, rather than everyday players who lack access to expensive equipment or coaching resources. 

## Personalized Training and Coaching Systems

Looking into a different area of literature, these works look into personalized or adaptive coaching systems. This is an important area as it is directly connected to these projects and their conversational and user-targeted design. In their 2024 review, Jud and colleagues explain that digital sports coaching and identifying personalization were among the strongest ideas of user engagement and performance improvement [@Jud2024_AIinDigitalSportsCoaching]. They also highlight other systems that use biometric sensors, motion tracking, and machine learning models to tailor plans [@Jud2024_AIinDigitalSportsCoaching]. While these strategies are helpful, Jud et al. (2024) also emphasize that challenges such as: most systems struggle to learn contextual factors such as motivation, environment changes, or equipment availability [@Jud2024_AIinDigitalSportsCoaching]. These are all areas considered in the building of CaddySense, and the goal is to overcome as many of these obstacles as possible. These ideas are especially relevant in golf, as factors like course layout, lie conditions, and club selection directly affect performance from session to session. In another work by Mohan et al. (2019) looked into AI-drieven coaching systems that were designed to back up exercise behavior, showing how AI could be used to support long-term user engagement through personalized feedback [Mohan2019_AIHealthCoach].

The idea of personalization becomes even more essential in tools that are structured around large language models (LLMs) for workout planning. Shin (2023), for example, introduces PlanFitting in his work and describes it as a system that uses LLMs to generate tailored plans for exercise based on specific user metrics [@Shin2023_PlanFitting]. This could be a promising system; however, Shin’s findings show that the results show that LLMs alone cannot replace domain reasoning. This means that the system often lacks awareness of real-world sports significance [@Shin2023_PlanFitting]. CaddySense addresses this issue by combining LLM feedback with structured golf performance metrics, which deliver recommendations backed up by domain-specific data. In this project in particular, metrics like handicap and approach shot proximity have acted as main structured anchors that are able to enhance the model’s reliability. 

The works of other researchers have expanded on this idea of personalization by including physiological feedback into their systems. Chen (2025) describes how biosensor-driven platforms adapt training intensity in real time [@Chen2025_PersonalizedTrainingThroughAI]. The findings back up that personalization is most effective when AI systems are able to incorporate both athlete-generated data and contextual signals [@Chen2025_PersonalizedTrainingThroughAI]. This is a principle that lines up with CaddySense’s design for locally stored, and also user-specific golf metrics. Local data storage ensures that the system reflects the golfer’s playing patterns rather than assuming them from drawn elite datasets.


In a broader sense, Rahmani and Majedi (2024) emphasize that adaptive models that are coaching systems must have some sort of balance between closeness with long-term training cycles [@Rahmani2024_ApplicationAIinSportsIndustry]. Raturi (2024) similarly explains that many AI systems prioritize shorter-term performance in the hands of athlete development [@Raturi2024_AIinSportsTrainingOverview]. CaddySense’s conversational aspect is different from these ideas because of how it is possible to contextualize short-term advice within long-term improvement plans.

Together, these studies as a whole provide two important limitations in personalized coaching tools that currently exist:

- They are lacking deep contextual understanding
- They rarely include sport-specific user-controlled data

Caddy Sense is specifically structured to overcome both of these ideas, to set it apart from these existing systems. CaddySense is built to prioritize user-owned data through the local SQLite-based storage and integrates a conversational reasoning system to accommodate the context that numerical measures by themselves cannot convey.

## AI Models and Performance Metrics

Performance metrics have always been a key factor when it comes to AI-driven sports analysis. In their article, Choudhary and Baladaniya (2025) describe how modern systems are able to integrate these metrics, such as workload, force output, and technical efficiency, in order to model pathways. Their review shows how performance modeling is most effective when the metrics are both interpretable and actionable [@Choudhary2025_AIinSportsScienceOptimization]. This review backs up the design of clear golf metrics that can be easily interpreted and explained. In golf, this means that emphasizing these metrics, such as driving distance, green in regulation, and more, can help all kinds of golfers find areas for improvement, and apply the findings to add into their practice plans.

Similarly, Mateaus et al. (2024) highlight that AI tools support scientific decision-making in training, recovery, and load management [@Mateaus2024_EmpoweringSportsScientistAI]. Their work also talks about how strong performance analytics depend on accurate models and other metrics that are aligned with real-world training priorities [@Mateaus2024_EmpoweringSportsScientistAI]. For example, approach shot accuracy is defined as how close a golfer lands their golf ball to the hole from outside 50 yards. This serves as a critical metric for mid to high handicap golfers.

Looking into the context of golf in specific, studies are often showing common measures of metrics like driving distance, green in regulation percentage, putting accuracy, accuracy off the tee, and wedge closeness. Even though none of these articles focused on golf, the collective literature suggests that these methods for translating sports metrics into computational models. Performance measures become the main structure of an adaptive system, which shapes both feedback generation and predictive modeling. Table 3 shows and gives a clear reference for the type of golf metrics that CaddySense uses in its design. This tool summarizes the variables that are apparent in the literature and proves why these metrics were chosen for this project.

Table: Common Golf Metrics used in AI Training Models

| Metric                      | Definition                                                                                |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Driving Distance            | Average yards hit from the tee box.                                                       |
| Green in Regulation (GIR)   | Percentage of holes where the golfer reaches the green in the expected number of strokes. |
| Average Putts per round     | Average amount of putts it takes a golfer to complete a round of golf.                    |
| Accuracy Off the Tee        | How often a player keeps the ball in the fairway.                                         |
| Approach Shot Proximity     | Distance to the hole on shots from 50+ yards out.                                         |

A work by Pietraszewski (2025) further shows that performance data from recreational athletes typically behaves differently from athletes of elite-level athletes [@Pietraszewski2025_RoleAIinSportsAnalytics]. These datasets are explained to show more variability and nonlinear progression, which shows that different levels of athletes progress at different times, making their adaptation to feedback different from each other [@Pietraszewski2025_RoleAIinSportsAnalytics]. This relates to my project, CaddySense, as it's designed for non-professional golfers who may be struggling with swings and other metrics, which makes their performance patterns different from assumed patterns in most models that already exist. This shows the need for adaptive systems that are capable of interpreting inconsistent data, rather than expecting perfect precision.

## User Trust and AI Interaction 

Even the most complex AI models are usually ineffective if the athletes using them do not understand or trust these AI systems. Wacholz et al. (2025) show the trust and the acceptance of AI-created exercise plans among recreational users [@Wachholz2025_TrustAIExercisePlans]. A conversational interface not only improves transparency but also allows users to go through the reasoning behind the recommendations they receive. This mirrors and acts more like natural dialogue between coaches and players [@Wachholz2025_TrustAIExercisePlans]. The results show two patterns throughout the study:

- Users are trusting systems more when feedback is conversational, adaptive, and transparent. 
- Trust trends down when AI is providing recommendations that are not backed up and are unexplained [@Wachholz2025_TrustAIExercisePlans].

These implications are the same for CaddySense. Many current systems of coaching mainly rely on scorecards, dashboards, or other kinds of analysis. CaddySense introduces an interface that is conversational, as well as allows users to ask questions, offer challenge recommendations, and request clarifications. The research from this work suggests that interaction at this level significantly improves engagement and long-term use [@Wachholz2025_TrustAIExercisePlans].

A different work from Passmore and Tee (2024) further shows how the combination of human and AI coaching models achieves the highest levels of engagement and trust when the AI works as a supportive figure rather than a demanding expert [@Passmore2024_SystematicReviewAIinCoaching]. Terblanche (2025) expands on this point by showing how health coaching systems are achieving better results when users perceive the AI as contextual, flexible, and accountable [@Terblanche2025_SystematicReviewHumanAIHybridCoaching]. By making explaining more obvious, along with optional detail, and user-led questioning, the system is designed to use that type of trust, which is key for long-term use by all kinds of golfers. These ideas are the main structure for AI systems that are not just technically sensible, but also fit for users' expectations, which is exactly what CaddySesne is specifically designed to accomplish.

## Ethical and Societal Context

Ethical concerns and considerations are seen across all the literature about the topics mentioned so far. For example, Gao in 2024 mentions and highlights the issues of fairness, transparency, and accessibility when it comes to sports training [Gao2024_AIinSportsEducationTraining]. The work argues that certain coaching technologies are risking the building up of existing qualities within the user, and questions if they are favoring elite athletes, or if they require expensive hardware [Gao2024_AIinSportsEducationTraining]. Rahmani and Majedi (2024) similarly note that AI systems are lacking cultural, financial, and infrastructural accessibility for the populations of athletes [@Rahmani2024_ApplicationAIinSportsIndustry]. These concerns are especially playing a key role in the sport of golf, as many commercial tools upload players' swings and their performance data to cloud servers, which are often lacking meaningful personalized feedback to the user.

Also in this work by Rahmani, the broader review of the industry also talks about potential data misuse and privacy, especially when AI systems rely on the storage of personal athletic histories [@Rahmani2024_ApplicationAIinSportsIndustry]. This is important for recreational athletes in particular, as they may be more careful with their privacy than professional athletes. Table 4 is included to make sure that these ethical problems are seen in CaddySense and make it easier to compare and see. This work also demonstrates how each risk discussed aligns with the design of this project.

Table: Ethical Risks in Sports and AI and how CaddySense Follows Them

| Ethical Issue                | Risk in Existing Tools                    | CaddySense's Structure                        |
|:-----------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| Data Privacy                 | Cloud upload exposes player data          | Local SQLite storage                          |
| Accessibility                | Tools focus on elite athletes             | Designed for recreational/elite players       |
| Transparency                 | Hidden metrics                            | Conversational explanations per output        |
| Cost Barriers                | Expensive hardware required               | User-controlled metrics and computation       |
| User Control                 | Limited ability to modify/delete data     | Full user-controlled data                     |

CaddySense targets and addresses these ethical implications by:

- Using SQLite, a local data storage.
- Giving user-driven access and control of personal information 
- Offers conversational explanation and interpretability 

These are the themes that are connected across the works of AI systems that are focusing on transparency, user interaction, and ethical measures, which are outside of just technical integration [@Rahmani2024_ApplicationAIinSportsIndustry]. By storing data locally in SQLite and avoiding the use of external servers, the system uses a more modern approach, while also following an ethical AI design.

## Summary and Research Gap

Even with these noticeable advances in AI-based coaching and performance analysis, there are many gaps that can be seen across all the literature that was reviewed in this chapter. These gaps include:

1. Recreational athletes are underrepresented in the design, deployment, and testing of AI coaching models
2. A lot of systems are currently relying on generic exercise models that do not have sport-specific knowledge
3. The personalization aspect is limited by there being a lack of contextual awareness and adaptive conversational areas.
4. Trust remains a steep obstacle, as systems currently provide vague and non-interactive feedback.
5. Ethical considerations, mainly around areas of privacy, data control, and accessibility, are ideas that are not addressed in the majority of current existing tools.

CaddySense sets out to bridge these highlighted gaps by focusing on a sport that has specific performance metrics, integrating a conversational AI to assist with trust and interpretability, and making sure that data is user-controlled. While accomplishing this, this project looks further beyond current research and personalized training and strives for a more personalized, adaptive coach that still follows all ethical implications and guidelines. This way, all athletes, no matter the skill level, can benefit from CaddySense. Overall, the system is designed not just as a performance tool, but also as an accessible, transparent, and user-directed coaching assistant that is built for the needs of all levels of golfers.
